query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys, the accelerated coupled degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is driven by the breakdown of locally protective oxide films on the more anodic phase at eutectic phase boundaries. Mechanical wear preferentially removes the protective oxide from these vulnerable regions, thereby exposing fresh metal and enhancing micro‐galvanic coupling between the distinct phases, which in turn accelerates local corrosion and further amplifies wear damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine lamellar microstructure with alternating phases (for example, a ductile fcc phase and a harder B2 phase) that possess inherent differences in electrochemical nobility and oxide stability.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical sliding wear and corrosive exposure (such as in a molten salt or aggressive aqueous environment) while maintaining an elevated temperature condition.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 450–650 °C), a corrosive medium that challenges oxide film stability, and mechanical wear applied in a controlled reciprocating sliding test.
generation.structural_mediator: The eutectic phase boundaries and interlamellar interfaces where differences in electrochemical potential lead to preferential oxide film breakdown and localized galvanic cells.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically disrupts the initially protective oxide layer on the more anodic phase. This exposes fresh, less-protected metal, which due to micro-galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries becomes more susceptible to corrosion. The ensuing localized corrosion further weakens the oxide scale, thereby creating a feedback loop that accelerates both wear and corrosive degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline where only wear or only corrosion occurs, the alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion will exhibit a markedly higher overall degradation rate, with deeper wear tracks and increased corrosion pit density. Each damage mode (wear and corrosion) will accelerate compared to their isolated counterparts due to the synergistic feedback between mechanical oxide removal and localized electrochemical attack.
generation.baseline: Control samples of the same eutectic HEA exposed separately to either mechanical wear only or corrosion only under identical elevated temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected in eutectic HEAs where the constituent phases have significantly different corrosion potentials and oxide stabilities. Alloys with a single homogenous phase or with negligible electrochemical contrast between phases likely will not exhibit the same degree of synergistic degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise acceleration factors and degradation rates depend on the specific alloy composition, microstructural scale, and the severity of the corrosive and mechanical environments. Quantitative predictions require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples from the same multiphase eutectic HEA. Subject set A to simultaneous wear and corrosion tests at elevated temperature, set B to wear only under the same mechanical and temperature conditions, and set C to corrosion only under the same environmental conditions. Use identical sample geometries and pre-test surface treatments across all sets.
measurements: Total mass loss over time using gravimetric analysis
Wear track depth and width via profilometry and microscopy
Corrosion pit density and depth via high-resolution imaging
Local electrochemical potential measurements to assess galvanic coupling at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation (mass loss, wear track dimensions, and corrosion pit characteristics) observed in the simultaneous wear and corrosion test (set A) is not significantly higher than the simple additive effects of wear only (set B) and corrosion only (set C), then the proposed synergistic mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
